topic.title: Service charge runs on shame
topic.claim: We pay restaurant service charge not because we agree with it, but because asking to remove it in front of friends costs more than the money.
topic.moment: The bill arrives with 10% service charge, someone notices, and nobody says a word.

turn.believed: It's a fixed part of the bill.
turn.actually: It's a charge that depends on you being too awkward to object.

topic.villain: Bills designed so the only way out is a public conversation
topic.because: The restaurant knows group dinners are about looking easy-going. Embarrassment does the collecting for them.
topic.payoff: Some charges are priced in rupees. This one is priced in awkwardness.
topic.behaviour: Groups split bills to the rupee on UPI but leave the service charge alone.
topic.mechanism: Social pressure makes a disputed charge feel compulsory.
topic.group: Young professionals who eat out with friends
topic.send_to: The friend who always pays the bill and secretly hates the service charge
topic.why_now: December means a season of group dinners and office parties.
topic.needs_facts: The current legal position on service charge in India (CCPA guidelines and court rulings), stated exactly as the sources state it

reader.point: People pay the optional restaurant service charge at group dinners because asking to remove it feels awkward and makes you look cheap, even though it's voluntary.
reader.reason: Removing it means someone has to ask out loud in front of everyone, and the social awkwardness costs more than the ₹200 share, so people pay to look easy-going.

sources.fact: A LocalCircles survey found 59% of consumers who ate at an air-conditioned restaurant in the past month paid a service charge, up from 43% in 2022. Only 16% got it removed.
sources.stance: neutral: The page shows many diners pay a charge that is meant to be voluntary. It does not ask why they pay, so it gives no evidence for embarrassment or social pressure.
sources.excerpt: 59% of consumers who went to an air-conditioned restaurant in the last one month paid a service charge.

sources.fact: The Delhi High Court held that service charge and tips are voluntary and cannot be made mandatory on food bills. It said the amount must not be added by default.
sources.stance: neutral: The page sets out the legal position that the charge is voluntary and should be left to the customer's discretion. It says nothing about social embarrassment or group dynamics. The ruling does make the post's point stronger, because the charge is legally optional and yet still paid.
sources.excerpt: service charge and tips are voluntary payments by consumers and cannot be made compulsory or mandatory on food bills. | mandatory collection of service charge on food bills is contrary to law | The amount however, ought not to be added by default in the bill/invoice and should be left to the customer's discretion. | puts the consumers under the impression that they are imposed in the form of service tax or GST.

paragraphs: In a LocalCircles survey, 59% of AC restaurant diners paid the service charge. One of them is you.
slides.why_swipe: If so many of us pay it, is it even optional?

paragraphs: The Delhi High Court already said it. Service charge is voluntary. It shouldn't even be on your bill by default.
Most of us know this. We pay anyway.
slides.why_swipe: Why do people who know still pay?

paragraphs: Whoever opens the bill folder first spots the line.
Their eyebrows go up for one second. Then, "chalo, theek hai."
slides.why_swipe: What does that one second actually cost?

paragraphs: Dinner for six comes to ₹12,000. The service charge is ₹1,200.
That's ₹200 each. Arguing over ₹200 makes you the cheap friend for a year.
slides.why_swipe: But is the group really that relaxed about money?

paragraphs: And these are the same friends who split the bill to the rupee on GPay.
But on this one line, suddenly nobody's counting.
slides.why_swipe: So why does that one line get a free pass?

paragraphs: To get it removed, someone has to ask out loud, in front of everyone.
And the waiter is standing right there, holding the machine.
slides.why_swipe: Who ends up paying for that silence the most?

paragraphs: It isn't carelessness. At a group dinner, we're paying to look easy-going.
And if you're the friend who always picks up the bill first, you've paid that price.
slides.why_swipe: So what are we really paying for?

draft.alt_text: An eight-card text post about restaurant service charge in India. It says that in a LocalCircles survey, 59% of AC restaurant diners paid the service charge, though the Delhi High Court has said it is voluntary and shouldn't be on the bill by default. It describes the group dinner moment when someone sees the charge line and stays silent, and the same friends who split bills to the rupee on GPay. It argues that removing the charge means asking out loud in front of everyone, with the waiter standing right there holding the card machine. It ends: some charges are priced in rupees, this one is priced in awkwardness.

claims.text: In a LocalCircles survey, 59% of AC restaurant diners paid the service charge.
The Delhi High Court said service charge is voluntary and shouldn't be on the bill by default.
The service charge on a ₹12,000 bill is ₹1,200, or ₹200 each for six people.
claims.derived_from: ₹1,200 service charge on ₹12,000; ₹1,200 / 6 = ₹200 (typical dinner for six at price-sheet levels)
